design_detail: Retrospective cohort built from statewide Utah medical records (1996–2011) linked to the Utah Population Database. People aged 30 or older at the end of follow-up were assigned by ICD-9-CM codes to a methamphetamine/amphetamine cohort (n=4,935), a cocaine cohort (n=1,867) or an unexposed population pool, and matched 5:1 on sex and birth year to controls with no drug or alcohol diagnosis (n=34,010 controls in total). Outcomes were a first coded diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (332.0) or a broader category also including secondary parkinsonism, other basal-ganglia degeneration and essential tremor (332.0, 332.1, 333.0, 333.1). Competing-risks (Fine-Gray) proportional-hazards models accounted for death.
can_establish: That people with a recorded stimulant-related diagnosis in Utah were later coded with Parkinson's disease or a related movement-disorder diagnosis about three times as often as matched people without any drug or alcohol diagnosis, while people with a cocaine-related diagnosis were not.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine causes Parkinson's disease: exposure is a diagnostic code with no dose, duration or route; the outcome is a code with imperfect positive predictive value at ages far younger than typical Parkinson's disease; the groups differ in healthcare contact, tobacco use, ethnicity and mortality; and the main comparisons are not adjusted for any of these.

sample.recruitment: Registry and health-system records, not volunteers: statewide inpatient discharge data plus outpatient records of the University of Utah and Intermountain Healthcare systems, which the authors say cover more than 80% of patient encounters in the state; 83% of the methamphetamine cohort and 77% of the cocaine cohort were identified within those two systems (Methods §2.1; Results §3.1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Born 1940 or later and aged at least 30 at the end of follow-up. Exposed cohorts required a stimulant-related ICD-9-CM code (methamphetamine/amphetamine: 304.4, 305.7, 969.7, E854.2; cocaine: 304.2, 305.6, 968.5, E855.2) and no code for any other illicit drug or for alcohol, no HIV code, and no movement-disorder diagnosis before the first stimulant code. Controls came from 1.43 million people with no drug, alcohol, HIV or prior movement-disorder code, matched 5:1 on sex and birth year, and required follow-up in Utah at least as long as their matched case (Methods §2.2).
sample.demographics: Table 1a. Methamphetamine cohort: median age at end of follow-up 40 (range 30–71) vs 42 in controls; mean follow-up 6.8 years (SD 4.3) vs 7.1 (4.3); median age at first exposure code 35 (range 15–69); 48.6% women; 87.0% recorded as white vs 94.2% of controls and 15.1% Hispanic vs 7.7%; 5.8% had died by the end of the study vs 0.4% of controls; a tobacco code was present for 58.6% vs 8.3%. Cocaine cohort: median age 43, 37.6% women, mean follow-up 8.0 years, 10.9% died. Sex-stratified figures are in Table 1b.
sample.attrition: Follow-up ended at the last recorded Utah event or death; deaths were handled as a competing risk. Of 16,931 people identified with a methamphetamine/amphetamine code, 11,985 (71%) were removed for any other drug or alcohol code and 11 for a prior movement-disorder diagnosis; of 7,952 with a cocaine code, 6,084 (77%) and 1 were removed on the same grounds.
sample.selection_effects: Exposure is only recorded for people whose stimulant use brought them into contact with the health system and was coded; controls are people without any such code, who may simply have had less contact or undiagnosed use. Restricting both exposed cohorts to people with no other drug or alcohol code removed about three-quarters of those identified, leaving an unusual group. Controls were required to have at least as long a Utah follow-up as their case, which selects for stable residence.

exposure.measurement: Presence of a stimulant-related ICD-9-CM diagnosis code in any diagnostic position in inpatient or outpatient records between 1996 and 2011. Within the methamphetamine cohort, 72% had the abuse code 305.7, 23% the dependence code 304.4, 5% a poisoning code and 14% codes in more than one category (Methods §2.2.2; Results §3.1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not available. No information on amount, frequency, duration, route, purity or whether use continued after the index code, so no dose-response analysis was possible.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by exclusion rather than adjustment: anyone with a code for another illicit drug or for alcohol was removed from both exposed cohorts. The authors note that use without a coded diagnosis cannot be ruled out, and report that among roughly 25,000 people with stimulant codes only 20% had both methamphetamine and cocaine codes. Tobacco was captured only by diagnosis codes (58.6% of the exposed cohort), which the authors say understates smoking, since self-reported smoking in a subset of 381 people was 78% (women) and 85% (men).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; no biological measurement at any point.

comparison.controls: Randomly selected people from the Utah population with no drug, alcohol or HIV diagnosis and no movement disorder at baseline, individually matched 5:1 on sex and birth year, with follow-up at least as long as their case. A cocaine cohort served as a second, drug-using comparison.
comparison.matching: Sex and birth year only. Not matched or adjusted for tobacco, ethnicity, healthcare utilization, socioeconomic position, psychiatric comorbidity or antipsychotic exposure. Tobacco adjustment appears only in a case-only comparison of the two drug cohorts.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No information on pre-exposure neurological status beyond the absence of a coded diagnosis, none on family history of Parkinson's disease, head injury, pesticide or other occupational exposure, or on premorbid prodromal features.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded by definition, but only as far as coding captures it; uncoded use is possible.

outcomes.instruments: ICD-9-CM codes in any diagnostic position: 332.0 for Parkinson's disease, and the broader combination 332.0, 332.1, 333.0 and 333.1 (secondary parkinsonism, other basal-ganglia degeneration, essential and other tremor). A limited subset of pharmacy data was inspected for carbidopa-levodopa orders.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors review the literature on the accuracy of these codes and report positive predictive values of about 57% for a single 332.0 code and 39% for 332.1 in one study, and 60–67% for the multi-code approach against 71–79% for 332.0 alone in another; they note that the commonest false-positive essential-tremor diagnosis is Parkinson's disease. No chart validation was done in this study.
outcomes.operationalization: Incident disease was defined as the first appearance of a qualifying code after 1 January 1996, including codes recorded on the same date as the first exposure code; a secondary analysis dropped those zero-interval cases.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated. Two outcome definitions, two exposures, overall and sex-stratified models, case-only comparisons and a zero-event-time sensitivity analysis are reported without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; outcomes come from administrative coding, which is independent of the research question but not of healthcare contact.

analysis.effect_sizes: Methamphetamine/amphetamine cohort versus matched controls: Parkinson's disease (332.0) 15 cases vs 27, HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8), P<10 to the minus 3; broader movement-disorder outcome 30 vs 49, HR 3.1, with the interval printed as 1.9–4.9 in the abstract and 2.1–4.5 in the Results. Sex-stratified for the broader outcome: women HR 5.0 (2.9–8.6), men HR 1.9 (1.1–3.5, P=0.03), with a non-significant case-only comparison of women against men. Cocaine cohort: 4 cases vs 22 controls, no increased risk (the hazard ratio appears only in Figure 2, an image). Case-only comparison, methamphetamine versus cocaine: HR 3.9 (1.4–10.8), P=0.01; after adding tobacco to that model the paper prints HR 1.9 with an interval of about 0.9 to 4.0 and P=0.01, apparently the coefficient for tobacco rather than an adjusted exposure estimate. Excluding people whose exposure and outcome codes shared a date: HR 2.2 (1.2–4.0) for Parkinson's disease and 2.3 (1.5–3.5) for the broader outcome. Editors' calculations from Tables 1a and 2 (absolute figures the paper does not give): Parkinson's disease in 0.30% of the exposed cohort vs 0.11% of controls, a difference of about 2 per 1,000 over a mean 6.8 years (about 4.5 vs 1.5 per 10,000 person-years); broader outcome 0.61% vs 0.20%, about 4 per 1,000 (8.9 vs 2.8 per 10,000 person-years). For the cocaine cohort the crude rates are indistinguishable (about 2.7 per 10,000 person-years in both). The female hazard ratio of 5.0 reflects 18 of 2,399 exposed women (0.75%) against 18 of 11,995 control women (0.15%).
analysis.covariates: The main case-control models used individual matching on sex and birth year with separate hazard functions per matched set, and nothing else. Case-only models adjusted for birth year and, where relevant, sex; one case-only model added tobacco. Race and ethnicity were deliberately not adjusted because categories would be sparse.
analysis.selective_reporting: Hazard ratios for the cocaine-versus-control comparison and the sex-stratified Parkinson's disease models appear only inside figures, which are images; the sensitivity analysis figures are in an online supplement. The tobacco-adjusted model is reported as data not shown.
analysis.power: Explicitly limited: 15 Parkinson's disease outcomes in the exposed cohort and 4 movement-disorder outcomes in the cocaine cohort. The authors state that power was insufficient for sex-stratified analysis of the narrow outcome and for the cocaine comparison, and that the sex difference was not statistically significant.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In administrative records, a stimulant-related diagnosis was followed by a Parkinson's disease or related movement-disorder code about three times as often as in matched people with no drug or alcohol code, on 15 and 30 events; the absolute excess was roughly 2 to 4 cases per 1,000 over about seven years. No comparable excess appeared after a cocaine-related diagnosis. Median age at the movement-disorder diagnosis was 49 in the exposed cohort and 44 in controls, the mean interval from the exposure code to the outcome code was about 2 years, and only 3 of the 30 exposed cases had a recorded levodopa order.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports a near three-fold increased risk that confirms prior observations and suggests risk may be higher than previous estimates, and the conclusion states the findings support the possibility that preclinical observations of Parkinson-like neurotoxicity are mirrored in humans, with profound implications for prevention and treatment. Those statements reach past what coded data can show: the outcome at these ages, with a two-year interval and almost no antiparkinsonian prescribing, is as compatible with detection of tremor or drug-related parkinsonism in people under medical observation as with neurodegeneration. The paper's own limitations section is candid about code accuracy, uncoded polysubstance use, antipsychotic exposure and the sex comparison, but the abstract and conclusions do not carry those qualifications, and the main hazard ratios are never adjusted for tobacco, which the authors identify as a confounder.

timeline.event: Small clinical study reporting more prolonged amphetamine exposure in people with Parkinson's disease aged 40–64 than in spouse controls (Garwood et al., 2006, as cited).

California hospital-discharge cohort: higher Parkinson's disease incidence after a methamphetamine-related admission than in an appendicitis comparison group, with no increase after cocaine-related admission
Review citing both registry studies as preliminary evidence consistent with damage in a subgroup, while noting that only a very small proportion of users is later diagnosed

replication.where_it_stands: Two independent record-linkage studies in different US states agree in direction and in the contrast with cocaine, which argues against pure drug-using-lifestyle confounding, but neither validated the diagnosis against charts, neither adjusted for smoking in the main comparison, and neither can measure exposure beyond a diagnostic code.

funding.funder: University of Utah Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology; US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA031883 (G. Hanson, principal investigator); partial support for Utah Population Database datasets from the Huntsman Cancer Institute and National Cancer Institute grant P30 CA2014. The funders had no role in design, analysis, interpretation, preparation or submission (Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (Author Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Utah (internal medicine, pharmacology and toxicology, family and consumer studies, dentistry), the Huntsman Cancer Institute, Intermountain Healthcare and the Utah Foundation for Biomedical Research. The senior author's laboratory works on stimulant neurotoxicity, which is the hypothesis under test. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: The same linkage with neurologist-validated diagnoses (chart review or a prescribing-based algorithm), longer follow-up into the age range where Parkinson's disease is common, measured smoking, adjustment for healthcare contact, and an exposure gradient from pharmacy or treatment records; prospective cohorts of people who use methamphetamine with standardized movement examinations and dopamine-transporter imaging would settle the mechanism.

key_findings.finding: People with a methamphetamine- or amphetamine-related diagnosis (n=4,935) had a higher hazard of a coded Parkinson's disease diagnosis than matched unexposed controls (n=24,675): 15 vs 27 events, HR 2.8 (95% CI 1.6–4.8).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results §3.2; Table 2 (Figure 1a holds the plotted estimates)

key_findings.finding: For the broader outcome (Parkinson's disease, secondary parkinsonism, other basal-ganglia degeneration or essential tremor): 30 vs 49 events, HR 3.1.
key_findings.note: The confidence interval is printed as 1.9–4.9 in the abstract and 2.1–4.5 in the Results; the two cannot both be right.

key_findings.finding: The cocaine cohort (n=1,867) showed no increased risk: 4 events vs 22 in 9,335 matched controls. Editors' calculation: about 2.7 per 10,000 person-years in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Results §3.2; Table 2 (the hazard ratio appears only in Figure 2, an image)

key_findings.finding: Case-only comparison: the methamphetamine cohort had a higher hazard of the broader outcome than the cocaine cohort, HR 3.9 (95% CI 1.4–10.8), P=0.01; adding tobacco to that model did not substantively change it, though the printed numbers are garbled.

Sex-stratified for the broader outcome: women HR 5.0 (2.9–8.6), men HR 1.9 (1.1–3.5, P=0.03); the direct case-only comparison of women with men was not significant. Editors' calculation: 18 of 2,399 exposed women (0.75%) vs 18 of 11,995 control women (0.15%); 12 of 2,536 exposed men (0.47%) vs 31 of 12,680 control men (0.24%).

Excluding cases whose exposure and outcome codes carried the same date left the result in the same direction: HR 2.2 (1.2–4.0) for Parkinson's disease and 2.3 (1.5–3.5) for the broader outcome; 3 of 15 and 8 of 30 exposed events were same-date.
key_findings.note: The P-value for the first of these is printed as P<10 to the minus 1, which does not match a confidence interval excluding 1.

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation of absolute risk from Tables 1a and 2: Parkinson's disease in 0.30% of the exposed cohort vs 0.11% of controls over a mean 6.8 years (about 2 extra cases per 1,000, roughly 4.5 vs 1.5 per 10,000 person-years); broader outcome 0.61% vs 0.20% (about 4 extra per 1,000).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation; the paper reports only hazard ratios.

key_findings.finding: Median age at the movement-disorder diagnosis was 49 (range 25–69) in the exposed cohort and 44 (20–68) in controls, and the mean interval from baseline to that diagnosis was 2.0 years (SD 1.8) in cases and 2.9 (3.5) in controls.
key_findings.note: These ages and intervals are far from the typical onset of idiopathic Parkinson's disease (about 60 years), which bears on what the codes captured.

key_findings.finding: Among people with an incident movement-disorder code, only 3 of 30 in the exposed cohort and 5 matched controls had a carbidopa-levodopa pharmacy order, from a limited subset of medication data.

A tobacco diagnosis was recorded for 58.6% of the exposed cohort against 8.3% of controls; the authors state this understates smoking, since 78% of women and 85% of men in a subset of 381 reported current or former smoking on questionnaires. The main hazard ratios are not adjusted for tobacco.

Cohort construction: 11,985 of 16,931 people identified with a methamphetamine/amphetamine code (71%) were excluded for having any other drug or alcohol code, and 6,084 of 7,952 (77%) in the cocaine group, so both cohorts represent people with a single coded substance.
Mortality during follow-up was 5.8% in the exposed cohort against 0.4% in controls (10.9% vs 0.8% for cocaine), handled as a competing risk in the Fine-Gray models.

reporting_issues.issue: The confidence interval for the broader outcome is 1.9–4.9 in the abstract and 2.1–4.5 in the Results for the same HR of 3.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any claim citing this interval must state which version; the precision of the headline estimate is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The tobacco-adjusted case-only model is printed with a malformed interval and an internally impossible combination: HR 1.9 with an interval that appears to run from 0.9 to 4.0 and yet P=0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether this is the tobacco coefficient or the adjusted exposure effect; the claim that tobacco adjustment does not change the result cannot be verified, and no tobacco-adjusted comparison with the population controls is reported anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity analysis excluding same-date cases reports HR 2.2 (1.2–4.0) with P less than 10 to the minus 1, a threshold inconsistent with an interval excluding 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Likely a typographical error for a smaller exponent; strength of evidence not readable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1b, women recorded as not white are given as 173 (1.2%) of 2,399; the percentage should be about 7.2%, as the three categories otherwise sum to more than 100 minus the stated values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic error in a table used to judge comparability of exposed and control groups.

reporting_issues.issue: Hazard ratios for the cocaine-versus-control comparison and for the sex-stratified narrow outcome appear only inside Figures 1a, 1b and 2, which are images, and the sensitivity-analysis figures are in a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several estimates cannot be extracted from the text; the cocaine null result has no printed interval, so its precision cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: Median age at end of follow-up differs between cases and controls (40 vs 42 overall) although matching was on birth year.
reporting_issues.consequence: Follow-up ended earlier for exposed people, consistent with their higher mortality; it also means exposed people were observed through slightly younger ages, when Parkinson's disease is rarer.

reporting_issues.issue: The broader outcome includes essential tremor (333.1), which the paper's own cited literature says is commonly confused with Parkinson's disease in both directions, and tremor is a recognized effect of stimulant use; no chart validation was performed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A share of the 30 exposed outcomes may be tremor or drug-related parkinsonism rather than neurodegenerative disease, which would inflate the hazard ratio for the broader outcome.

domains.note: Matched only on sex and birth year. Tobacco (58.6% vs 8.3% coded), ethnicity, healthcare contact, psychiatric comorbidity and antipsychotic exposure are unadjusted in the main models. Smoking would bias the estimate downward, surveillance and antipsychotic exposure upward, so the net direction is unclear.
A diagnostic code with no dose, duration, route or recency; uncoded use misclassifies controls; exposure requires coded health-system contact.

Population-based with contemporaneous controls and a residence-based follow-up algorithm, which is a strength, but about three-quarters of people with stimulant codes were excluded for other substance codes.
Antipsychotic and other dopamine-blocking medication, which can produce parkinsonism, was not measured; the authors say this was beyond scope.
Administrative data with near-complete capture within the state; loss to follow-up handled by the residence algorithm and death as a competing risk.

ICD-9-CM codes with reported positive predictive values of roughly 57–79% depending on definition, no chart validation, an outcome category that includes essential tremor, a median diagnosis age of 49 and only 3 of 30 cases with a recorded levodopa order.

Two outcome definitions, several subgroup and case-only models and a sensitivity analysis without multiplicity control; some estimates only in figures or marked data not shown; the abstract and Results disagree on one interval.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is a genuine strength: a whole-state population, contemporaneous matched controls, outpatient as well as inpatient capture, a cocaine comparison group that argues against generic drug-lifestyle confounding, and death handled as a competing risk. But the exposure is a code and the outcome is a code of modest accuracy, recorded at ages and intervals that do not fit idiopathic Parkinson's disease, and the central estimates are unadjusted for tobacco and healthcare contact. The association is real in the records; its interpretation as drug-induced neurodegeneration is not established.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4295903 (accepted author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1a, 1b and 2 as text, figure legends, funding, disclosure and contributor statements; Figures 1a, 1b and 2 are images carrying several hazard ratios, and the supplementary .docx and two .tif sensitivity figures were not opened because they are downloads)
